items.title: Manufacturer fined after worker suffers life-changing injuries in conveyor incident
items.summary: Maintenance engineer suffered catastrophic, life-changing injuries after his arm was pulled into an unguarded conveyor Working alone, he waved at a CCTV camera for help after becoming trapped in the machinery Factory Services UK Limited fined £160,000 after pleading guilty to health and safety breaches A Merseyside animal‑feed manufacturer has been sentenced after a maintenance […]
items.body:
- Maintenance engineer suffered catastrophic, life-changing injuries after his arm was pulled into an unguarded conveyor
- Working alone, he waved at a CCTV camera for help after becoming trapped in the machinery
- Factory Services UK Limited fined £160,000 after pleading guilty to health and safety breaches
A Merseyside animal‑feed manufacturer has been sentenced after a maintenance engineer suffered severe, life‑changing injuries when his arm was drawn into an unguarded conveyor.
An investigation by the Health and Safety Executive (HSE) found that Factory Services UK Limited allowed workers access to dangerous parts of machinery for many years at its site on Moorgate Road, Deacon Park, Knowsley Industrial Park, L33 7RX.
On 18 March 2025, maintenance engineer Daniel Slinger was working a nightshift when he was asked to look at an issue on a conveyor. While the conveyor was still running, Mr Slinger reached through a hole in the side of the conveyor casing to clear away some material. His arm was pulled into the moving machinery. There was no guard in place and no emergency stop button in the area.
Working alone at the time, there was nobody nearby to see or hear what had happened. In an effort to raise the alarm, he repeatedly waved at a CCTV camera in the hope that someone monitoring the system would spot him and come to his aid, nobody did. Eventually, after 40 seconds, he was able to free his arm. This was despite the company’s own safe systems of work requiring machinery to be guarded and isolated before any maintenance or cleaning activity was carried out.
Mr Slinger suffered catastrophic injuries to his forearm and hand, including a fracture and extensive degloving. He required multiple operations, blood transfusions and continues to receive ongoing specialist treatment. He remains unable to return to work.
HSE’s investigation established that the hole had been cut into the conveyor years earlier to allow workers to clear blockages while the machine remained in operation. A second conveyor on site was also found to have a similar unauthorised access point. Despite routine inspections, management walkarounds and audits, the dangerous modifications had not been identified or rectified.
Following the incident, the company fitted a fixed mesh guard and installed an emergency stop button at the location.
Factory Services UK Limited pleaded guilty to breaching Section 2(1) of the Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974 at Warrington Magistrates’ Court on 8 September 2026. They were fined £160,000 and ordered to pay costs of £4728.
Following the hearing, HSE Inspector, Ian Betley, said:
“Mr Slinger suffered devastating and life-altering injuries as a result of this preventable incident. Had the correct protections been in place he would not have been exposed to the dangerous parts of a running conveyor through a hole cut into the machine.
“Factory Services UK Limited had risk assessments and safe systems of work, but they were not followed or enforced. Employers must ensure guarding is properly maintained, safe systems are implemented, and workers are protected from foreseeable risks.”
This prosecution was brought by HSE enforcement lawyer Alan Hughes and paralegal officer Henrietta Ruthven.
Further Information
- Guidance on the safe use of work equipment, including guarding requirements, can be found here: https://www.hse.gov.uk/pubns/books/l22.htm
- Further details on the latest HSE news releases are available at: https://press.hse.gov.uk/
- HSE does not pass sentences, set guidelines or collect fines. Sentencing guidelines for health and safety offences can be found at: https://www.sentencingcouncil.org.uk/sentencing-and-the-council/about-sentencing-guidelines/about-published-guidelines/health-and-safety-offences-corporate-manslaughter-and-food-safety-and-hygiene-offences/

items.title: Next Retail Limited & Anor v M Thandi and Ors
items.body:
Judgment approved by the Court for handing down Next Retail Ltd v M Thandi & Ors
Rolls Building
Fetter Lane, London, EC4A 1NL
Before :
THE HONOURABLE MR JUSTICE BOURNE
Between :
1) Next Retail Limited
2) Next Distribution Limited
Appellants
-and-
Miss M Thandi and others
Respondent
Patrick Green KC, Kathleen Donnelly KC, Chloe Campbell, Thomas Mallon (instructed by Eversheds Sutherland International LLP) for the Appellant
Andrew Short KC, Gus Baker (instructed by Leigh Day) for the Respondent
Hearing dates: 16 – 17 June 2026
JUDGMENT
Summary
Sex Discrimination & Equal Pay
In respect of the employer’s appeal against the Employment Tribunal’s finding that it had not made out the material factor defence under section 69(1)(b) of the Equality Act 2010 with regard to the difference between the claimants’ and the comparators’ basic pay (and some other benefits):
The Employment Tribunal did not err in finding that the claimants had shown particular disadvantage because of the statistical differences between the claimant and comparator groups together with its other findings of fact.
However, it erred in finding that the employer did not pursue a legitimate aim when setting different rates of pay. The aim, taken as a whole, of paying higher rates to warehouse staff included recruitment and retention factors which did not apply to the claimant group. It was not necessary for the employer to justify not increasing the claimants’ pay to the same level.
Its alternative finding that the employer’s reliance on a material factor was not a proportionate means of achieving a legitimate aim therefore could not stand, and in any event it erred in the assessment of proportionality when analysing the market forces factor, and in focusing on the reasons for the claimants’ lower pay and the affordability of increasing it rather than on the reasons for the comparators’ higher pay.
There was no error of law in the Employment Tribunal’s analysis of some of the other pay benefits.
In respect of the claimants’ cross-appeal, the Employment Tribunal did not err when finding that there was no direct discrimination contrary to section 69(1)(a) of the 2010 Act. In particular:
It is not the case that direct discrimination must always be found where an employer relies on a material factor of market forces and does not adduce evidence to prove that those market forces do not disadvantage those of either sex.
There was a sufficient evidential basis for the findings as to the employer’s reasons for its decisions despite the employer not calling evidence from a Board member or adducing documentary evidence stating the reasons.
THE HONOURABLE MR JUSTICE BOURNE:
Introduction
This judgment deals with an appeal and a cross-appeal against a decision of the Leeds Employment Tribunal (Employment Judge Jones, Mr Roberts and Ms Fleming, “the ET”) which was sent to the parties on 22 August 2024.
I shall refer to the parties respectively as “the claimants” and “Next”, the latter term referring interchangeably to the two respondents to the ET proceedings.
The claims were brought by 3,540 retail sales consultants working in Next’s shops. In 2018 they brought claims under the equal pay provisions of the Equality Act 2010 (“the 2010 Act”), complaining that they were paid less than the comparators, all of whom are operatives in Next’s warehouses where goods are processed and sent to stores for sale or to customers who have made purchases online.
By an earlier decision dated 2 June 2023 the same ET had ruled that the work of three lead claimants was of equal value to that of four named comparators, and that decision is binding on all parties.
Next relied on what is known as the “material factor” defence. The ET hearing of that issue, relating to a period from 2012 to 2023, occupied 15 days in May and July 2024. The ET considered whether the defence was established in relation to 20 distinct contractual pay terms or categories. The most important is basic pay. The others are various entitlements including certain bonuses and premiums.
The ET decided that Next’s defence failed in respect of basic pay and six other terms or categories. In the case of four terms or categories it decided that there was no difference between the pay of the claimants and the comparators. It decided that the defence succeeded in respect of the other nine terms or categories.
Statutory framework
Chapter 3 of the 2010 Act is entitled “Equality of Terms”.
Section 64 applies the relevant provisions where “a person (A) is employed on work that is equal to the work that a comparator of the opposite sex (B) does”.
The word “equal” in that context is defined by section 65. Under section 65(1) it covers three types of case, namely cases where A’s work is “like B’s work” or is “rated as equivalent to B’s work” or, materially for the present case, it is “of equal value to B's work”. In that regard the section provides:
“(6) A's work is of equal value to B's work if it is—
(a) neither like B's work nor rated as equivalent to B's work, but
(b) nevertheless equal to B's work in terms of the demands made on A by reference to factors such as effort, skill and decision-making.”
The mechanism adopted by the legislation in section 66 is, in effect, to insert a “sex equality clause” into “the terms of A’s work”, so that:
“(2) Where this section applies by virtue of section 64(1), a sex equality clause is a provision that has the following effect—
(a) if a term of A's is less favourable to A than a corresponding term of B's is to B, A's term is modified so as not to be less favourable;
(b) if A does not have a term which corresponds to a term of B's that benefits B, A's terms are modified so as to include such a term.”
So, if A is paid less than B for work of equal value, the sex equality clause operates to give A a legal entitlement to be paid the same as B. That entitlement is enforceable by the Employment Tribunal under section 120 of the 2010 Act.
However, the entitlement is subject to section 69 which is the key provision for this appeal. It provides so far as material:
“(1) The sex equality clause in A's terms has no effect in relation to a difference between A's terms and B's terms if the responsible person shows that the difference is because of a material factor reliance on which—
(a) does not involve treating A less favourably because of A's sex than the responsible person treats B, and
(b) if the factor is within subsection (2), is a proportionate means of achieving a legitimate aim.
(2) A factor is within this subsection if A shows that, as a result of the factor, A and persons of the same sex doing work equal to A's are put at a particular disadvantage when compared with persons of the opposite sex doing work equal to A's.
…
(6) For the purposes of this section, a factor is not material unless it is a material difference between A's case and B's.”
The “responsible person” by section 80 includes A’s employer. Successful reliance by the employer on section 69 is what is referred to as the “material factor” defence.
The issues before the ET
Having established that the claimants were paid less than the comparators and that the work was of equal value, the ET was charged with applying section 69 as a matter of fact and law. That meant answering the following questions:
Was the difference in pay because of a material factor?
If so, did Next’s reliance on the material factor involve treating the claimants less favourably because of their sex than it treated the comparators?
If not, could the claimants show that, as a result of the factor, they and persons of their sex were put at a particular disadvantage when compared with comparators of the opposite sex?
If so, was reliance on the factor a proportionate means of achieving a legitimate aim?
Next relied on some or all of six material factors to explain the difference in respect of each term:
Market forces and market price, which the ET found to mean, in essence, “paying the going rate”.
Recruiting and retaining sufficient warehouse labour.
Maintaining 24/7 work in the warehouse, including night shifts, overtime, Sundays and public holidays.
Incentivising high productivity within the warehouse, generally and during peak periods of demand.
Incentivising consistent and high attendance in the warehouse, in particular during peak periods of demand.
Business viability, resilience and performance of the NEXT Group and subsidiaries.
In order to apply section 69 to the factors, the ET adopted a (more or less) agreed list of issues which addressed the questions listed at paragraph 14 above in more detail.
First the ET considered whether reliance on the factors involved treating the claimants less favourably because of their sex than the comparators. That question has been paraphrased as meaning whether there was direct discrimination on grounds of sex by Next, e.g. by knowing that the retail work was perceived as “women’s work” and the warehouse work was “men’s work” and being content to take advantage of that perception and of its impact on the pay differential.
The ET then considered in the alternative whether reliance on the factors was shown by statistical evidence to put the claimants at a particular disadvantage compared with the comparators. This is sometimes referred to as Enderby discrimination. I shall return to the Enderby case below.
The claimants also had originally mounted a case based on showing that indirect discrimination arose from provisions, criteria or practices (“PCPs”) associated with each type of work which put women at a disadvantage, but that case was not pursued.
If any factor was found to put the lead claimants at a particular disadvantage, Next then contended that each factor was justified as a proportionate means of achieving a legitimate aim, those aims being:
Viability, resilience and successful business performance.
Maintaining 24/7 warehouse work.
Incentivising warehouse productivity.
Incentivising consistent and high warehouse attendance.
In the list of issues, this yielded the following “key factual issues”:
“8.9 Was the market price for the lead claimant and comparator roles different and specifically was it higher for comparator roles?
8.10 Was it necessary to pay the market price for comparator roles in order to recruit and retain sufficient warehouse labour?
8.11 Was it legitimate and proportionate not to pay sales consultants a rate which was above that required to sufficiently staff retail stores?
8.12 Does the rationale for paying premium pay to warehouse operatives who work night shifts, Sundays and public holidays apply in the same way to sales consultants?
8.13 Were the bonuses paid to the comparators linked to the productivity of the recipient?
8.14 Are the matters alleged by the claimants as to the market rates being affected by gender breakdowns of the relevant job groups and being ‘sex tainted’ and allegedly ‘inherently discriminatory’ ‘differentials’ relevant considerations as a matter of law and if so how do they affect the legitimacy or proportionality of any of the matters relied on by the respondents in respect of objective justification?”
The background facts
Having heard very extensive evidence, the ET in its clear and thoughtful judgment identified relevant facts including the following.
In 2012/13 Next operated 540 shops in the UK, selling clothing and in some stores home and garden items. By 2023 the number of shops had fallen to 466.
The number of sales consultants was 32,351 in 2013 (working 23 million hours annually) and had fallen to 22,873 by 2023 (working 16.5 million hours).
Retail sales were £2,191 million in 2013, falling to £1,865 million in 2023. Retail profits grew from £331 million to £402 million between 2013 and 2016, then fell to £164 million by 2020. In 2021 there was a loss of £206 million. Retail profits were £107 million in 2022 and £241 million in 2023.
Next operates nine main warehouses, all of which are in Yorkshire. The four comparators worked at the Elmsall complex or DVB. These locations variously serve the retail parts of the business and mail order and online orders.
The number of warehouse operatives was 3,550 in 2013 (working 6.5 million hours), rising to 6,478 today (working just over 10 million hours in 2023). Agency workers accounted for different percentages of the work at different times ranging from 16% in 2013 to 8% in 2023.
Between 2013 and 2023, online sales rose from £1,193 million to £3,007 million and online profits rose from £302 million to £467 million.
Each year, proposals for retail pay rates were included in a retail budget which would be established by the Head of HR for Retail and the senior management team in retail. This would be submitted to the Finance Department which would prepare budgets for the year, including remuneration proposals, for approval and sign off by the Board.
Pay rates were also discussed by an “influential” body known as the People Focus Meeting which included Next’s CEO Lord Wolfson, the Director of HR, the Retail Sales Director and/or Head of HR for Retail and the Retail Finance Manager. It was attended by Next’s principal witness on the retail side, its Group HR Director Lionel Mason.
In the years 2012-2015 a pay review took place each February. Rates would be introduced in Autumn to take account of changes in the National Minimum Wage (“NMW”) which took effect in October. In 2015 and 2016 the review date was moved to October and April respectively to align with the changing dates when increases to NMW took effect.
For warehouse operatives, there was a formal recognition agreement with USDAW as the sole trade union for employees below supervisor level at the second respondent’s distribution centres. It provided for Next to negotiate with USDAW in respect of basic pay, weekly hours of work and holidays at specifically convened meetings.
The Director of Warehousing set the operating budget and pay levels, and set the optimum target pay rates for any annual increase in conjunction with the Head of HR and the Head of Finance. Agreement with the CEO and the Group Operations Director was then obtained with respect to the budget and target level of remuneration increase before the meetings with the USDAW negotiating committee commenced. These would typically take between 2 and 4 days, before a Joint Statement was agreed and voted upon by the union membership.
Sales consultants were primarily recruited via Next’s careers website, with others coming from other websites where Next posts vacancies or from direct contact with a store, referrals or social media. Next calculates the number of staff required by an analysis of the demand for work. Agency staff were not required. Business needs were met by permanent and fixed time staff who would cover additional shifts through a facility known as Shift Market Place which operated until February 2022 and which allowed staff to manage their own shifts on a week by week basis.
For the relevant period up to 2015, there were between 28 and 30 applications per vacancy for retail store workers. In 2019 the average number of applicants per vacancy was 33. There were wide variations between stores, ranging from two in St Peter Port, Guernsey to 258 in Oxford Street. After the Covid lockdown there was a significant increase in the number of applications per vacancy.
During the relevant period Next used recruitment platforms and spent much greater sums to recruit a sufficient number of warehouse staff. It also used agency workers to fill work demands, these accounting for approximately 10% of warehouse operative hours.
At the Elmsall and DVB sites, warehouse staff hours increased from 2.9 million in 2012 to 5.6 million in 2023, and the numbers of agency staff rose from 741,909 to 836,792 in 2023. Significant numbers of workers were recruited from EU countries, particularly Poland, though these had a high attrition rate.
Financial incentives were introduced to aid recruitment of warehouse operatives.
The difference between the hourly rate of basic pay of sales consultants and warehouse operatives was £0.92 in 2012. The differential was reduced by the introduction of the national living wage in 2017. By 2023 it had reduced to £0.38.
There was a difference between the gender profile of the retail and warehouse workforces.
Over the relevant period 77.5% of retail consultants were female and 22.5% were male, with small variations between years and particular locations.
Over the relevant period an average of 47.22% of warehouse operatives were female and 52.78% male. At the Elmsall Complex an average of 48.25% of operatives were female and 51.75% male. At DVB, an average of 47.13% of employees were female and 52.87% were male. For most periods at Elmsall and DVB the gender split has been within 5%, for many years within 3% and in some years within 1%.
There was also a difference between the profile of part-time workers in the two workforces. On average 96% of retail staff were contracted to work fewer than 30 hours, and the average number of weekly hours per retail worker was 14 over the relevant period.
Conversely, over the relevant period 53.65% of warehouse operatives worked part-time and 46.35% full-time. From 2016, more warehouse operatives had part-time roles than full-time roles (ranging from 51.92% to 61.31% throughout the period 2016 to 2023). Within those, 36.8% of warehouse operatives were working fewer than 30 hours and 26% fewer than 20 hours.
The ET identified a document produced by the second respondent in 2018 which included a breakdown of part-time and full-time work by gender for one day. According to that document, 47% of the female workforce worked part-time compared with 21% of the male workforce.
The ET’s findings on the issues
The ET’s judgment addressed basic pay first and then returned to the other contested terms, and it is convenient to take the same approach here.
Having found that the basic pay of the comparators was at all times higher than the basic pay of the lead claimants, the ET found that the factors explaining the difference were factors 1 and 2 and the more generic factor 6. It was clear that pay generally was set by reference to the prevailing rates in the respective markets for sales consultants on the one hand and warehouse operatives on the other, which were very different marketplaces that had attracted different rates of pay for various reasons. In particular (paragraph 201), it was clear that “there were specific pressures in the market for warehouse operatives, particularly in the area of recruitment, which did not arise in the marketplace for sales consultants”.
The ET found that factor 6 must be applied carefully and not too liberally, but that (paragraph 202):
“… the setting of basic pay during the relevant period was intended by the respondents to maintain both sectors of the business. This included managing a reduction in high street sales because of changes in shopping habits in the retail marketplace with a corresponding increase in warehouse provision”.
The claimants had argued that the pay of retail consultants was “suppressed” for historically discriminatory reasons, including the appeal of store work to female workers and the preponderance among them of part-time workers who earned a secondary income to support the main household breadwinner, and that Next had not shown that it had not been influenced in any way by these factors. However, the ET found (paragraph 208) that the difference in pay did not involve less favourable treatment because of the sex of the lead claimants:
“The evidence of Mr Mason, Mrs MacIntyre and Mr Kelly was compelling. It was all about cost. Gender did not enter into the equation. Historic reasons for imbalances in pay for work which is equally valued fall into indirect discrimination considerations. There was no conscious or subconscious influence of gender which affected the basic rates of pay. The drive and imperative was to reduce cost and enhance profit. That would have happened regardless of the gender split in either market, even had there been more men than women sales consultants or women than men warehouse operatives. The renegotiation of the warehouse contracts in 2017, such that new starters had less beneficial rates than existing staff, was reflective of that state of mind. In that market, men were in the majority.”
The ET therefore ruled that there was no “direct discrimination”, i.e. section 69(1)(a) was satisfied. The ET turned to the “indirect discrimination” question under section 69(1)(b).
To establish that as a result of the material factors, they and other women doing equal work were put at a particular disadvantage, the claimants relied on statistics. In Enderby v Frenchay Health Authority [1994] ICR 112 (“Enderby”), the European Court of Justice ruled at paragraph 19 that:
“Where significant statistics disclose an appreciable difference in pay between two jobs of equal value, one of which is carried out almost exclusively by women and the other predominantly by men, article 119 of the EEC Treaty requires the employer to show that that difference is based on objectively justified factors unrelated to any discrimination on grounds of sex.”
The ECJ explained the point in its judgment:
“16. If the pay of speech therapists is significantly lower than that of pharmacists and if the former are almost exclusively women while the latter are predominantly men, there is a prima facie case of sex discrimination, at least where the two jobs in question are of equal value and the statistics describing that situation are valid.
17. It is for the national court to assess whether it may take into account those statistics, that is to say, whether they cover enough individuals, whether they illustrate purely fortuitous or short-term phenomena, and whether, in general, they appear to be significant.”
The ET referred to Home Office v Bailey [2005] ICR 1057 (“Bailey”) for the proposition that “significant” is not a high hurdle, though it recognised that the question of whether the statistics were sufficient was “not entirely straightforward” in this case. It noted that pay levels had been set by benchmarking against a market which did not differentiate between warehouses which were predominantly male and those in e-commerce fulfilment centres where, as here, there was a smaller difference or no difference. It held that the statistics, together with the benchmarking point and the gender balance of part-time workers of whom there were many among the sales consultants (and the discussion in Dobson v North Cumbria Integrated Care NHS Foundation Trust [2021] ICR 1699 (“Dobson”) about the convenience of part-time work for many female workers) satisfied section 69(2). There was therefore a finding of “particular disadvantage” and Next was required to justify its reliance on the material factors as a proportionate means of pursuing a legitimate aim.
The relevant aim was the first in the list at paragraph 20 above: “Viability, resilience and successful business performance”.
Having found (at paragraph 245) that factors 1, 2 and 6 were an “appropriate means” of achieving the aim, the ET asked itself whether paying the unequal basic pay was “reasonably necessary”, balancing the business need against the discriminatory effect. It found that paying the market rate to warehouse workers was necessary and that Next “could not reduce this without a risk of jeopardising the required service from warehouses” (paragraph 247).
However, it went on:
“248. Mr Short says that does not justify paying the lower rates to the sales
consultants. The impact upon the retail staff was that they were not receiving a similar level of remuneration in their basic pay for doing equal work. Although the hourly difference was less than a pound and reducing over the relevant period, the marginal purchasing power of such sums should not be underestimated for pay rates at this level.”
The ET noted Next’s response, that it was working within a budget to maintain efficiency and the fact that the NMW paid to the retail workers was itself above what the market rate would otherwise have been, and also that retail workers benefited from certain non-wage amenities such as higher staff discount, a wardrobe allowance and the convenience of Shift Marketplace to which I have referred, which were not available to warehouse staff.
It did not give weight to Next’s further point that any claimant could choose to transfer to one of its warehouses and that there had been very low take-up of a redeployment opportunity to do precisely that, though it noted certain “positive aspects” of the retail work.
The parties’ positions were crystallised at paragraph 260 of the ET’s judgment:
“Paying a higher rate of basic pay to sales consultants which was not necessary from a commercial perspective would come at a cost to the business and impact on the profitability of the first respondent and the NEXT Group. The claimants say cost cannot be advanced as an excusable defence to discrimination and if market forces prevailed in such cases it would defeat the purpose of the legislation.”
The ET directed itself to case law on the question of whether and when reliance on market forces is a proportionate means of achieving a legitimate aim, notably Heskett v Secretary of State for Justice [2021] ICR 110 (“Heskett”), to which I return below, and extracted the principle that adopting a measure “solely to avoid increased costs” will not, without more, amount to achieving a legitimate aim. The ET used the phrase “costs alone” to describe that impermissible approach, and to its converse as “costs plus”, though it acknowledged that the Court of Appeal in Heskett cautioned against an inappropriately mechanistic approach which could arise from using those terms.
In the key passage for present purposes, the ET concluded:
“269. There is no real scope for any costs plus ingredient, when the whole drive was about cost saving, a consistent theme of the relevant witnesses. We recognise in the broadest sense that business decisions in this industry were not just about making profits. High street shopping has been on the wane leading to the closure of stores and the loss of retail jobs over a sustained period. The claimants pointed out in closing submissions that there was no evidence the reduction in stores was the reason retail wages were held at or near national living wage rates. But the first respondent has survived where many other retailers have gone to the wall. This was achieved by careful management, particularly in the field of budget planning. Difficult decisions made by businesses are not made with full foreknowledge of the headwinds and so what may appear to be ungenerous wage settlements yesterday may transpire to have avoided business failure today. The fact that the first respondent has made sustainable profits throughout the period, save for the year after lockdown, and could absorb the cost of the same basic pay for work of equal value is a judgment the Tribunal can pass with the merciless wisdom of hindsight. All that said, we are satisfied that with respect to basic pay the legitimate aim of viability, resilience and successful business performance [aim 1], fairly characterised, falls on the wrong side of the demarcation line, of costs only, with no element of costs plus.
270. Even were we wrong, and this were a permissible aim, the payment of different sums of basic pay, for the factors, was not reasonably necessary to meet it. The business need was not sufficiently great as to overcome the discriminatory effect of lower basic pay, having regard to all the considerations we have explained above, including the financial headroom and having given all due allowance for the non-wage amenities in retail. Mr Short is correct to say that for market forces to be a trump card in this way would defeat the objective of the legislation; lower pay in particular sectors due to indirectly discriminatory practices could then be lawfully sustained in perpetuity. There must usually be a more compelling business reason for such arrangements to be justifiable, such as with the incentivised productivity bonuses we consider below.”
For those reasons the section 69 defence was not established in respect of basic pay.
The ET then turned to the other terms. The section 69 defence succeeded in respect of some of them. In brief:
Payment of an additional 10% for about 11 weeks to workers who returned to the warehouse early from furlough after Covid (term 1) was justified, where there was no equivalent need to incentivise a return by retail workers who returned two months later in sufficient numbers.
Payment of a “peak premium bonus” to warehouse workers for 3 months (also term 1) was justified when this was to fend off a crisis arising from Amazon offering significantly higher pay to new warehouse operatives in the same area, and there was “no comparative crisis” arising from competition for retail workers.
Payment of an attendance bonus of £1,000 to warehouse workers at Elmsall for 100% attendance in a three month period in 2021 (term 3) was justified. This again was paid because of “aggressive competition” from Amazon in that location and “no comparable problem arose in the retail sector”.
Under terms 6, 7 and 8, “sophisticated” bonus schemes for warehouse workers, which mostly rewarded enhanced productivity, were justified. They achieved a type of “cost incentivisation” which could not be applied to the different duties of the retail workers and there was no duty on Next to devise some other scheme to equalise their pay.
It was justified to pay public holiday premium i.e. enhanced rates for working on public holidays to warehouse operatives with a start date before 1 February 2017 (terms 11 and 12), given the difficulty of finding sufficient warehouse staff to work on those days and the lack of comparable difficulty in attracting sales assistants on those days.
It was justified to pay an Additional Hours Premium (term 13B) to warehouse staff at Elmsall only, around Christmas 2021 (the busiest time of the year), following operational disruption caused by Covid. There was no business need for such payment at DVB. Nor was there such a need in respect of the retail staff.
The ET found no material difference between the terms of the claimants and the comparators, and therefore no need to decide the section 69 issues, in the case of holiday bonus (term 9), bank holiday bonus (term 10), holiday entitlement (term 14) and holiday pay (term 15).
The section 69 defence was not established in relation to the following (in addition to basic pay):
Unconsolidated Awards (term 2) were lump sum payments to warehouse staff negotiated with USDAW to conclude deals. These enabled Next to preserve lower rates of basic pay. Although the collective bargaining context did not apply to retail staff, the aim was found to be “essentially … cost saving” and therefore not legitimate. Had it been legitimate, factors 1, 2 and 6 would have been a proportionate means of achieving it.
Historically, warehouse and retail staff had received a Sunday Pay Premium at varying rates (term 4). It was removed from warehouse workers for new starters from 2017 onwards but those entitled to it under their existing contracts continued to receive it. It was removed from retail workers for new starters from October 2008 onwards, and from all retail workers from June 2015. This reflected a move in the market away from enhanced Sunday pay. Following that market trend was a legitimate aim. However, the evidence did not support a difficulty in attracting warehouse staff to work on Sundays, so the business need was not sufficient to outweigh the discriminatory effect of the differential pay.
Both warehouse and retail staff could earn a Night Time Premium (term 5) for working at night. This was key to warehouse operation and the premium was paid for work from 10pm to 6am.The shops were not open at night but during sale periods they opened from 5am. From November 2012, hours worked between midnight and 5am, rather than 6am, were classified as night time, and that difference was just to save costs which was not a legitimate aim. The differences also were not proportionate, not being justified merely by differences in operational requirements.
Overtime Premium (term 13A), where applicable, was more generous for warehouse staff. Although there was no business need for overtime in retail, proportionality required that the terms should be equivalent “to cover the eventuality that overtime might, exceptionally, be required in retail”.
Paid rest breaks (term 16) were provided for warehouse staff. For retail staff they had been removed following the introduction of NMW. Although unpaid rest breaks might be an “industry standard” in retail, the payments were removed for an aim which was “solely about cost” and therefore was not legitimate. Nor would the removal have been found proportionate as it was not reasonably necessary.
Long Service Awards (term 17) were more generous for warehouse staff than for retail staff. The differences arose from negotiation with USDAW on an overall pay package for the warehouse staff. Although they arose from a legitimate aim of meeting business need, there was no good reason not to equalise the payments and so the difference was not justified.
The grounds of appeal
Next’s appeal
As was explained in the skeleton argument of Patrick Green KC (with Kathleen Donnelly KC, leading Chloë Campbell and Thomas Mallon) (Footnote: 1), the “essence” of the appeal is:
“… that the Employment Tribunal wrongly found that NEXT should have paid Retail Sales Consultants the same Basic Pay as Warehouse Operatives, to whom a completely different rationale for paying more applied, effectively because NEXT could afford to do so”.
There are, nevertheless, 16 discrete grounds of appeal. That reflects the searching and detailed analysis to which Next’s counsel have subjected the ET’s decision, though it must be said that it has not made this Tribunal’s task easier.
Grounds 1-15 are grouped under the headings of Legitimate Aim (grounds 1-7), Particular Disadvantage (grounds 8-10) and Proportionality (grounds 11-15).
Those grounds contend that there were errors of law under those headings in relation to basic pay, and that some of the same or similar errors were made in respect of some of the other pay benefits in respect of which the claim succeeded.
By ground 16, Next further contends that the ET made specific errors of approach in respect of pay terms 4, 5, 16 and 17.
The pleading of the 16 grounds occupies 23 pages. Rather than lengthening this judgment by reproducing them, I shall attempt to identify the core of each ground in the discussion below.
The claimants’ cross-appeal
The cross-appeal is directed only against the ET’s finding under section 69(1)(a) that the difference in pay was because of a material factor reliance on which “does not involve treating A less favourably because of A's sex than the responsible person treats B”.
By ground 1, Andrew Short KC (leading Gus Baker) contends that the ET erred by limiting itself to a consideration of the internal conscious or subconscious attitudes, intentions or mental processes of Next’s decision makers and should instead have found that the market forces relied on were themselves affected by stereotypes which were discriminatory on grounds of sex.
By ground 2, they contend that the ET’s finding that there was no conscious or subconscious influence of gender on the setting of basic pay was perverse because there had been no evidence from the relevant decision-makers and the relevant documents were not produced.
Appeal grounds 8-10: Particular disadvantage
I take these grounds first because, under section 69, the issue of particular disadvantage is a hurdle which a claimant must clear before the tribunal is required to consider whether the material factor is a proportionate means of achieving a legitimate aim.
Next’s submissions
By ground 8, Next contends that the ET “was not entitled to ‘make good the claimants’ case under section 69(2)’ as it purported to do”. That is on the premise that the ET had rejected the claimants’ expert evidence on this issue and had “implicitly held” that the claimants could not establish particular disadvantage by statistics alone.
By ground 9, Next essentially contends that the ET erred by confusing the warehouse market against which it had benchmarked pay (e-commerce fulfilment centres in Yorkshire) with the national warehouse market within ONS Code 9252, characterising this as “a warehouse market with a largely male workforce” (judgment paragraph 239).
By ground 1o, Next contends that the ET erred in its consideration of what has been called the “childcare disparity” and its application of Dobson, making a speculative finding that the childcare disparity was the reason why many workers had chosen to work as sales consultants and failing to assess the causal relationship between the disparity and the pay differential.
Mr Green KC submitted that caution was necessary when the ET decided whether the statistics were sufficient to establish particular disadvantage. At paragraph 234 its observation that the question was “not entirely straightforward” was correct, but Mr Green criticised the next part of that paragraph:
“However, the fact the respondents repeatedly set their remuneration levels by benchmarking against the market is significant. That market did not differentiate between those warehouses which were predominantly made up of men, and those in ecommerce fulfilment centres in which the differential was more finely balanced or there was no gender difference at all. Taking the market as a whole, there is a significant imbalance favouring men. The ONS data for 2012 to 2021 shows over 80% of men worked in elementary storage occupations. The setting of pay by that means therefore reflected a predominantly male based labour market.”
Mr Green submitted that the finding that Next benchmarked pay against the market and did not distinguish between warehouses with different gender profiles was conjecture, and that the ONS warehouse code was wrongly treated as relevant when it included data about many types of workers – such as fish lumpers and cold storage workers – whose work was completely different from that of Next’s warehouse employees. The latter point gives rise to ground 9.
Mr Green then objected to paragraph 239 where the ET concluded:
“We are satisfied the statistics, the fixing of pay by benchmarking in a
warehouse market with a largely male workforce, the gender make-up of those who did part-time work, as above, together with the considerations in Dobson make good the claimants’ case under section 69(2). The influences Mr Green has drawn attention to, whilst material, are not of comparable weight or significance. But they remain relevant to issues of proportionality to which we return.”
Here, he said, the ET had disregarded factors to which he had drawn its attention, such as the fact that there was a higher proportion of female managers in Next’s warehouses and, regardless of the fact that the claimants had the burden of proving particular disadvantage, had impermissibly “made good” their case for them. That was ground 8.
Furthermore, Mr Green submitted that the ET wrongly applied the case of Dobson, giving rise to ground 10. Instead of merely taking notice of the fact that part-time work is often more convenient for female workers because of childcare responsibilities (“the childcare disparity”), it made an incorrect and unfounded assumption that female workers would have a strong preference for a working week of 14 hours (the average in the shops) over a working week of 20 hours (the ET found that from 2016, 36.8% of warehouse workers worked less than 30 hours and 26% less than 20 hours). The over-ready inference of particular disadvantage from the childcare disparity was something against which this Tribunal warned in Dobson itself at paragraphs 50 and 51 (to which I return below).
The claimants’ submissions
In response, Mr Short reminded me that particular disadvantage can be found in a case of the Enderby type where there is “a sufficiently substantial disparity in the gender breakdown of the two groups”: Newcastle upon Tyne NHS Hospitals Trust v Armstrong [2010] ICR 674 (“Armstrong no.2”) per Underhill P at paragraph 20. Such a disparity, he submitted, existed in this case. The key point is the difference between the make-up of the two groups, whereas Next in this case has chosen to focus on the proportions of men and women in the comparator (warehouse) group only. He cited the example of Grundy v British Airways plc [2008] IRLR 74 where a disparate impact was found even though both claimant and comparator groups were predominantly female (66% in the advantaged group, 95% in the disadvantaged group).
Mr Short also reminded me of Bailey, where the Court of Appeal rejected the idea of a “high threshold” for a disparity which would establish a prima facie case of indirect discrimination, bearing in mind that it would remain open to the employer to justify the disparate impact on the basis of a material factor.
In summary, Mr Short submitted that the ET directed itself correctly as to the law and arrived at conclusions of fact which were, at the very least, open to it on the evidence. As to the facts, he pointed out that the evidence showed Next regularly benchmarking the pay of warehouse workers by comparison not only with similar types of warehouse involving “picking” e-commerce items, but also with more traditional types of warehouse, especially those of large supermarket chains. Mr Short accepted that the ONS categories to which the ET referred included some activities which were different from those in Next’s warehouses, but noted that those categories had nevertheless been relied on for comparison purposes by Dominic Miles, an expert witness called by Next in the ET to give an opinion on market rates for the two roles, who in cross-examination had said:
“… when we looked at the description under the ONS SOC codes for what those were, they appeared to align reasonably well with job adverts, descriptions of the role. So to that extent we thought they were reasonably representative.”
In respect of the childcare disparity and Dobson, Mr Short submitted that the ET did not make the error of just assuming that gender disparity translated into particular disadvantage. Instead, it examined the relevant working hours and commented on the evidence before drawing rational conclusions.
Accordingly he submitted that the ET’s factual conclusion was not perverse and contained no error of law.
Discussion
Bailey was a claim under Equal Pay Act 1970 (“the 1970 Act”) by administrative and executive staff in the Prison Service. They claimed equal pay with comparators in other grades such as prison officers and governors. The claimants’ employee group contained roughly equal numbers of men and women whilst the comparator group were predominantly men. Statistics showed that only 9% of men, compared with 51% of women, were in the disadvantaged group. The ET held that the statistics made out a prima facie case of indirect discrimination, placing a burden of justification on the employer. The EAT allowed an appeal, holding that where there was no barrier to women becoming members of the advantaged group, there was no prima facie discrimination unless the disadvantaged group was predominantly female. The Court of Appeal allowed the claimants’ appeal, holding that the statistical approach was valid and that it was not necessary to show a barrier to entering the advantaged group (a “requirement or condition”).
The Court of Appeal held that the Enderby statistical approach applied equally to cases where indirect discrimination was said to arise from a requirement or condition and those where there is simply a disparity in pay between two groups of workers. At paragraph 30 Peter Gibson LJ said:
“I can see no justification for the imposition of a high threshold for satisfying the test of prima facie discrimination. Where, as here, there is one group of employees of an employer which contains a significant number, even though not a clear majority, of female workers whose work is evaluated as equal to that of another group of employees of the employer who are predominantly male and who receive greater pay, it would be very surprising if an employment tribunal were to be precluded by the presence in the disadvantaged group of a significant number of men from holding that that disparity in favour of men required justification by the employer. In the present case it may well be that, as the Home Office suggests, there is a genuine material factor which is not the difference of sex and which justifies that disparity. Whether there is such factor is for further determination.”
At paragraph 39 Waller LJ added:
“… the above leads me to the view that section 1(3) cannot demand a high threshold for the establishment of a disparity which prima facie is due to sex. Thus where a difference in pay is established, and statistics seem to indicate a possibility of a disproportionate impact on women when looking at both the advantaged and disadvantaged groups as a whole, those statistics must provide sufficient evidence to get those carrying the burden over the hurdle of placing the onus on the employer to show that there were material factors which were not the difference in sex. For the reasons given by Peter Gibson LJ in my view the employment tribunal was entitled to reach the conclusion it did.”
Mr Green urged me to be cautious in applying Bailey, which of course predated the 2010 Act. It seems that an appeal to the House of Lords in Bailey would have considered the question of the evidential threshold for showing prima facie discrimination but the case settled. See the discussion in Villalba v Merrill Lynch & Co Inc [2007] ICR 469 at paragraph 123 per Elias P.
Be that as it may, grounds 8-10 do not put forward any submission that Bailey was wrongly decided.
Meanwhile, I do not agree with Mr Green that the ET in paragraph 239 made an implied finding that the statistics in the present case were not sufficient to show particular disadvantage. The ET said that it was persuaded by those statistics plus other factors, and it is a moot point whether it would have been so persuaded in the absence of the other factors.
I therefore reject ground 8. The phrase “make good” does not mean that the ET embarked on some impermissible exercise of supplementing an inadequate case advanced by the claimants.
Instead, I agree with Mr Short that it was open to the ET to be persuaded by the statistics. The statistical case was not of the overwhelming kind, as the ET acknowledged at paragraph 234. But there was a clear difference, of the kind identified in Armstrong no.2, between the gender profiles of the advantaged and disadvantaged groups.
In the event, the ET did not rely on the statistics alone, as I have said. Its conclusion was bolstered by the findings relating to benchmarking and those relating to part-time work.
So far as benchmarking is concerned, I am not persuaded that the ET’s reference to ONS data bears the weight which Mr Green sought to place on it. The ET did not suggest that the work in Next’s warehouses is closely comparable to the work in the national warehousing sector considered as a whole. Instead, it found that Next’s pay rates were influenced, to an unspecified extent, by benchmarking against a market in which no clear distinction was drawn between e-commerce fulfilment centres and other warehouses of a male-dominated kind. The fact that the latter sector contains fish lumpers and others whose work is very different from that of Next’s employees is not the point. The point is that the benchmarking exercise “reflected a predominantly male based labour market” (judgment paragraph 234).
The finding that that benchmarking took place was a finding of fact. Although ground 9 alleges “irrationality”, it does not allege that the finding of fact was perverse. And, as Mr Short said, the evidence clearly did show that the benchmarking exercise did not confine itself to e-commerce fulfilment centres.
I therefore reject ground 9.
Turning to ground 10, Dobson was a claim for indirect discrimination on grounds of sex. The claimant was subjected to a PCP requiring her to work flexible hours including at weekends. The ET found that although this disadvantaged her, there was no evidence of disadvantage to women as a group. Allowing her appeal, the EAT ruled that (1) the ET had wrongly identified the relevant pool of workers among whom to make the comparison and (2) it should have taken judicial notice of the fact that women bore a greater burden of childcare responsibilities than men and that this could limit their ability to work certain hours. On that basis the case was remitted for rehearing. However, Choudhury P added:
“… taking judicial notice of the child care disparity does not necessarily mean that the group disadvantage is made out. Whether or not it is will depend on the interrelationship between the general position that is the result of the child care disparity and the particular PCP in question. The child care disparity means that women are more likely to find it difficult to work certain hours (e g nights) or changeable hours (where the changes are dictated by the employer) than men because of child care responsibilities. If the PCP requires working to such arrangements, then the group disadvantage would be highly likely to follow from taking judicial notice of the child care disparity. However, if the PCP as to flexible working requires
working any period of eight hours within a fixed window or involves some
other arrangement that might not necessarily be more difficult for those with child care responsibilities, then it would be open to the tribunal to conclude that the group disadvantage is not made out. Judicial notice enables a fact to be established without specific evidence. However, that fact might not be sufficient on its own to establish the cause of action being relied upon. As is so often the case, the specific circumstances will have to be considered and one needs to guard against moving from an ‘indisputable fact’ (of which judicial notice may be taken) to a ‘disputable gloss’ (which may not be apt for judicial notice) … . It does not seem to me that the ET simply jumped from a finding that many retail workers worked part-time to a finding that paying lower rates to that group placed women at a particular disadvantage. Instead, when deciding whether the statistical difference between the two groups demonstrated particular disadvantage, it found (1) that the breakdown of hours (in judgment paragraph 235) justified an inference that women have been attracted to the working hours available in the shops and (2) that this, to an unspecified extent, supported the finding of particular disadvantage based on the statistics.
The question is whether that finding involved a misdirection or error of law. In my judgment it did not. The ET had regard to the “specific circumstances” as required by Dobson, making a comparison between the working hours of the two groups, having regard to the gender profile of the two groups and also considering other potentially relevant factors (in paragraph 236). Whilst it was not bound to draw an inference that childcare responsibilities will have been a relevant factor, in my judgment it was justified in doing so.
It seems to me that requiring much more by way of evidential foundation for the inference would blunt the force of the ruling in Dobson, and requiring much more by way of granular explanation of the inference would risk overstepping the role of this Tribunal in reviewing ETs’ factual findings.
I therefore also reject ground 10, and do not overturn the finding of particular disadvantage.
