Discussion
In my judgment, the ET made some of the errors attributed to it by Mr Green when it decided that Next did not pursue a legitimate aim when setting the different rates of basic pay.
It is necessary to emphasize that legitimate aim and proportionality are two separate questions. The ET set out its decision on proportionality at paragraph 270 of its judgment to which I return below. But at paragraph 269, it concluded that Next’s aim was fairly characterised as “costs only, with no element of costs plus”.
The reason given, in summary, was that “the whole drive was about cost saving”, in circumstances where Next “could absorb the cost of the same basic pay for work of equal value”, that latter point being a judgment passed by the ET “with the merciless wisdom of hindsight”.
It seems to me that this case illustrates a potential difficulty which is liable to arise when section 69 is applied in practice.
The purpose of the section is to determine whether the reason for a difference between A’s and B’s contract terms is discrimination (direct or indirect) on grounds of sex. The statutory route involves identifying (1) any material factor being relied on and (2) any legitimate aim being pursued by that reliance. It also involves deciding whether the reliance amounts to direct discrimination, whether the factor puts those of one sex at a particular disadvantage and if so, whether the reliance is a proportionate means of achieving the aim.
The potential difficulty is caused by tribunals (and the parties in their pleadings) having to distinguish between factors, aims and reliance on factors, treating those things as separate entities and subjecting them to separate tests, when in many cases the factors, aims and reliance will all just amount to one thing, namely the employer’s reason for having different terms for different employees.
That in my view is reflected by the comment in Heskett about the need for a “fair characterisation of the employer’s aim taken as a whole”. In the present case at least, it was necessary to consider the “aims” and the “factors” together.
The ET found at paragraph 245 that setting pay rates on the basis of the factors of market forces, recruitment and retention and overall business viability, resilience and productivity were an appropriate means of achieving the aim of “viability, resilience and successful business performance”, and at paragraph 247 that Next could not reduce the warehouse market rate without a risk of jeopardising the required warehouse service.
On the basis of those findings, it is inescapable that Next’s aim in setting the warehouse rates, fairly characterised as a whole, encompassed the need to recruit and retain sufficient staff to maintain the warehouse service.
At that point in the judgment, the ET referred to Mr Short’s submission that this did not justify paying a lower rate to the retail workers and then went on to discuss proportionality. But at paragraphs 265-269, it homed in on the issue of legitimate aim and “costs only” versus “costs plus”.
There, in my judgment, the ET fell into the error of requiring an employer to identify the aim of paying lower pay to the retail staff instead of identifying the aim of the difference in pay between retail and warehouse staff. Its approach was contrary to the guidance given in the last words of paragraph 85 of Heskett quoted above:
“… It is legitimate for a public authority (or indeed any employer) to seek not to make payments to employees to whom the rationale for those payments does not apply …”.
On the ET’s findings of fact, Next needed to pay the higher market rate for warehouse work, not because of gender but because of recruitment and retention factors. That rationale did not apply to the retail workers. So as in Bainbridge, whilst it “might be said” that the employer’s aim in not evening up the pay of the disadvantaged group was to save the cost of having to do so, “that was not the whole story”.
Another case taking a similar approach was Woodcock v Cumbria PCT [2012] ICR 1126, to which Underhill LJ referred in Heskett. The claimant was dismissed for redundancy and his employer timed the notice of dismissal to expire before his 50th birthday, when he would have been entitled to early retirement on an enhanced pension. On his claim for age discrimination, the Court of Appeal held that the employer had served the notice for the legitimate aim of giving effect to its genuine decision to terminate his employment on the ground of his redundancy, and not “with the aim, pure and simple” of saving expense. It was a legitimate part of the aim to ensure that the dismissal also avoided the extra expense which would have been incurred if it had not been timed as it was.
The same approach can be seen in Rainey and Blackburn which are summarised above and whose common theme is that although the employers saved the expense of giving the claimants treatment equal to that of the comparators, the aim of (or the reason for) the more favourable treatment of the comparators was something other than saving expense, and was something which did not apply to the claimants.
And, as the case of Benson shows, whilst financial considerations will be relevant in the analysis of proportionality at the next stage, the employer’s aim of allocating its resources is not rendered illegitimate by the fact (if proved) that it could have afforded to allocate them differently.
For these reasons I have concluded that the ET was wrong to find a lack of legitimate aim. The error was as described in grounds 1-4 and 6.
I am not persuaded that ground 5 adds anything. It is based on internal inconsistency, rather than on analysis of the ET’s reasoning relating to basic pay. However, I agree that it is not altogether clear why the ET found the same aim to be legitimate in respect of some terms when it was not legitimate in respect of basic pay.
Appeal Grounds 11-15: Proportionality
Next’s submissions
I have already quoted paragraph 270 of the ET’s judgment where it ruled that the business need to rely on the material factors was insufficient to overcome the discriminatory effect of lower basic pay, having regard to matters including Next’s “financial headroom”. It accepted a submission that for market forces to be a “trump card” in this way would defeat the objective of the legislation, sustaining lower pay which existed in particular sectors because of indirectly discriminatory practices. Next had failed to prove the “more compelling business reason” which was present in the case of some of the bonus (etc) arrangements on which the ET found in its favour.
Mr Green began by submitting that the exercise of deciding whether Next’s reliance on the material factors was a proportionate means of pursuing a legitimate aim was vitiated by the errors – set out above – in identifying and characterising that aim. If the aim was not correctly identified, or was wrongly characterised as confined to cost cutting, then the right proportionality question was not asked.
That, Mr Green suggested in his skeleton argument, “appears to have distracted the Tribunal, to select affordability or ‘financial headroom’ as the metric by which to assess proportionality”.
Similarly Mr Green contended that the assessment of proportionality was vitiated by the errors identified in grounds 8-10 in respect of Particular Disadvantage, although I have now ruled against him in respect of those grounds.
Ground 11, therefore, is that the ET’s approach to proportionality was vitiated by earlier errors.
By ground 12 Mr Green argued that the ET misdirected itself in its construction of section 69 and its conclusions about market forces being used as a “trump card”.
He first referred to Enderby, where the third question put to the ECJ was whether or to what extent a pay differential can be justified where part of it is attributable to a shortage of candidates for one job and the need to attract them by higher pay. The Court at the very least recognised that reliance on market forces can be justified. See paragraphs 26-28 of the judgment, quoted at paragraph 117 above, and the conclusion:
“29. The answer to the third question, therefore, is that it is for the
national court to determine, if necessary by applying the principle of
proportionality, whether and to what extent the shortage of candidates
for a job and the need to attract them by higher pay constitutes an
objectively justified economic ground for the difference in pay between
the jobs in question.”
In the present case, he submitted, the ET erred by assuming that because the statistics showed particular disadvantage, unlawful discrimination was made out in the absence of a “more compelling business reason” which could justify the differential, instead of considering whether the particular disadvantage could in fact be justified. That, he said, was contrary to the guidance of Lady Hale in Essop v Home Office [2017] ICR 640at paragraph 29 (dealing with the justification of indirect discrimination):
“There is no finding of unlawful discrimination until all four elements
of the definition are met. The requirement to justify a PCP should not be seen as placing an unreasonable burden upon respondents. Nor should it be seen as casting some sort of shadow or stigma upon them. There is no shame in it. There may well be very good reasons for the PCP in question … .”
Accordingly, Mr Green contended that Next’s case did not involve market forces being treated impermissibly as a trump card. Whether reliance on market forces justifies a pay differential must always be decided on the facts, and the ET was wrong to assume that if market forces were a permissible material factor, then reliance on them would always make out the defence.
But, he submitted, paragraph 27 of Enderby (quoted above) makes clear that if the employer explains the whole of the differential by reference to market forces, and shows that it has a genuine need to pay what the market demands, the test is satisfied. That was the case here, where the ET found that Next paid no more than the market rate to the comparators and could not have paid less without jeopardising the service, while also paying the claimants the NMW which exceeded what would have been the market rate for their work.
Mr Green also contended that the ET’s rejection of market forces as a material factor justifying the difference in basic pay was irrational, given its acceptance that market forces did justify differential pay in respect of terms 1, 11, 12 and 13B.
By ground 13, he argued that the finding at paragraph 270 was irrational or plainly wrong in light of the ET’s findings of fact that there were specific pressures in the market for warehouse staff, the overall remuneration package was designed to assist the recruitment problems, the labour budget for warehouse staff was subject to cost control and the basic pay for Next’s warehouse staff was “in the lower quartile of the market”.
Ground 14 alleges a failure by the ET to assess the extent, if any, to which the difference in basic pay was caused by any discriminatory effect.
Ground 15 alleges a failure to appreciate the difference between the relatively nuanced facts of this case and the facts of (1) a case like Enderby with more stark statistics or (2) an indirect discrimination claim under section 19 where the 2010 Act requires that there be “no material difference” between the circumstances of each case or (3) an equal pay case under section 65(1)(a) which is based on “like work” rather than work which is not the same or broadly similar but has been found to be of equal value, or (4) a case based on a PCP where a barrier to entry to work is identified.
In support of those grounds, Mr Green referred to Hardy & Hansons plc v Lax [2005] EWCA Civ 846, [2005] ICR 1565. That case included a claim for indirect discrimination on grounds of sex by a female employee who, in pregnancy and after maternity leave, was not allowed to switch to part-time work. The ET found that the employer’s PCP in this regard would be to the detriment of a considerably larger proportion of women than men and was to her detriment, and that the employer had failed to justify it. Dismissing an appeal, Pill LJ (with whom Thomas and Gage LJJ agreed), described the objective justification test:
“32. … The employer has to show that the proposal, in this case for a full-time appointment, is justified objectively notwithstanding its discriminatory effect. The principle of proportionality requires the tribunal to take into account the reasonable needs of the business. But it has to make its own judgment, upon a fair and detailed analysis of the working practices and business considerations involved, as to whether the proposal is reasonably necessary. I reject the employers' submission … that, when reaching its conclusion, the employment tribunal needs to consider only whether or not it is satisfied that the employer's views are within the range of views reasonable in the particular circumstances.
33. The statute requires the employment tribunal to make judgments upon systems of work, their feasibility or otherwise, the practical problems which may or may not arise from job sharing in a particular business, and the economic impact, in a competitive world, which the restrictions impose upon the employer's freedom of action. The effect of the judgment of the employment tribunal may be profound both for the business and for the employees involved. This is an appraisal requiring considerable skill and insight. As this court has recognised in Allonby [2001] ICR 1189 and in Cadman [2005] ICR 1546, a critical evaluation is required and is required to be demonstrated in the reasoning of the tribunal. In considering whether the employment tribunal has adequately performed its duty, appellate courts must keep in mind … the respect due to the conclusions of the fact-finding tribunal and the importance of not overturning a sound decision because there are imperfections in presentation. Equally, the statutory task is such that, just as the employment tribunal must conduct a critical evaluation of the scheme in question, so must the appellate court consider critically whether the employment tribunal has understood and applied the evidence and has assessed fairly the employer's attempts at justification.
34. The power and duty of the employment tribunal to pass judgment on the employer's attempt at justification must be accompanied by a power and duty in the appellate courts to scrutinise carefully the manner in which its decision has been reached. The risk of superficiality is revealed in the cases cited and, in this field, a broader understanding of the needs of business will be required than in most other situations in which tribunals are called upon to make decisions.”
Mr Green submitted that in the present case the ET did not carry out the necessary “critical evaluation”. It did not measure the actual disparate impact which fell to be justified (see also his submissions on Particular Disadvantage). It also did not discuss the implications of evidence that, for example, there were about 30 applicants for every store job, or the fact that the NMW being paid by Next to store workers was above what the market rate would have been. It did not mention the fact that some of Next’s competitors insulate themselves against this sort of claim by outsourcing their warehouse operation. And it did not comment at all on the important evidence which they had heard about Next fixing its budgets with regard to the viability of individual stores, as opposed to just assessing business needs at an aggregate level.
On that basis Mr Green invited me to carry out the necessary careful scrutiny of the ET’s decision, having regard to a sufficient understanding of “the needs of business”, and to find that the ET’s evaluation was insufficient.
The claimants’ submissions
Here again, Mr Short submitted that the purposes of equal pay legislation include the overriding of market rates which are discriminatory, and that this has been confirmed by a consistent line of case law to which he referred in his skeleton argument when dealing with the claimants’ cross-appeal:
In British Coal Corporation v Smith [1994] ICR 810 (Footnote: 2) at 858C–D, Balcombe LJ said that when an employer seeks to show objective justification under section 1(3) of the 1970 Act:
“Nor does the employer show a ‘material factor other than the difference of sex’ if he has adopted a criterion which is itself discriminatory, i.e., tainted by gender. If ‘market forces’ are relied upon, he must show that these are gender-neutral if he is to succeed in establishing the defence.”
In North Yorkshire County Council v Ratcliffe [1995] ICR 833 (“Ratcliffe”), an employer re-engaged female employees on a lower rate, paying them less than it paid men for work of equal value, in order to compete with a commercial business which discriminated against women in its pay rates. Lord Slynn said at 841C–D that the reduction of an overwhelmingly female job group’s wages in response to competitive pressures “was the very kind of discrimination in relation to pay which the Act sought to remove.” It was not necessary for the applicants to show that the competitor consciously discriminated against women.
In Armstrong v Newcastle upon Tyne NHS Hospital Trust [2005] EWCA Civ 1608, [2006] IRLR 124, Arden LJ referred to that passage in Ratcliffe:
“It was not necessary for the applicants to show that the reason why competitors paid dinner ladies less than the applicants’ comparators was because they consciously discriminated against women. As Lord Slynn observed, in the passage I have already cited, to permit employers to rely on market forces as the reason for reducing women’s pay below that of their male comparators would be to permit the very kind of discrimination the 1970 Act sought to redress. In equal pay cases, it is necessary at all times to keep in mind the overarching social and economic purposes of the legislation.”
In Middlesbrough Borough Council v Surtees [2007] ICR 1644, Elias P held at [49] to [50]:
“It is important to bear in mind the purpose of the legislation and in particular the fact that there are structural reasons causing unequal pay. There has historically been much stereotyping of jobs with assumptions being made both about what work is suitable for men and women and what pay is appropriate to those jobs. This has led to much de facto job segregation … That history continues to leave its mark on pay structures. Tribunals must be alive to the very real possibility that where there is adverse impact, identified where necessary by sufficiently cogent statistics, that may be the result of factors which are sex tainted… .”
In Armstrong No.2, the EAT found that an employer had failed to justify a discriminatory pay differential which had continued after it had ceased to correspond to a real business need. At [65], Underhill P said that he had found applying decisions including Ratcliffe “peculiarly difficult”, but:
“… we are prepared to say that we do not regard the outcome of the appeal as surprising. We agree with both Lord Slynn and Arden LJ that the 1970 Act might be expected to give a remedy in cases of this kind; and we see nothing odd in the conclusion that the trust had failed to justify a differential which had continued for so long after its initial rationale had disappeared.”
In response to ground 15 and to Mr Green’s point that a case involving work of equal value should be distinguished from one involving employees engaged on the same or similar work, Mr Short referred to Dumfries and Galloway Council v North [2013] ICR 993, where Lady Hale at [34] referred to work requiring physical strength having traditionally been better paid than those requiring dexterity and noted that one of the objects of equality legislation is “to iron out those traditional inequalities of reward where the work involved is of genuinely equal value”, with no indication that any distinction should be drawn between the different categories of comparable work.
With that introduction, Mr Short reminded me that justification involves an evaluative exercise by the ET which should not be interfered with on appeal in the absence of a misdirection or other error of law or a perverse finding. He submitted that none of those things can be found in the ET’s judgment. Although the conclusion on proportionality was stated briefly at paragraph 270, it was supported by all of the findings and reasoning from paragraph 246 onwards. The ET, he submitted, reached conclusions which it was entitled to reach.
On that basis he invited me to reject the contention in ground 11 that there were errors which vitiated the proportionality exercise. As to ground 12, he submitted that there was no error in the reference to a “trump card”. As North and other cases show, equal pay legislation makes it unlawful to apply “going rates” which are themselves discriminatory. With respect to ground 13, Next could not surmount the high hurdle of showing perversity and, having explored the facts in great detail, the ET was entitled to find that there was no sufficiently compelling business need to justify the pay differential.
In answer to ground 14 – the alleged failure to assess the extent to which the difference in basic pay was caused by any discriminatory effect – Mr Short submitted that this ground misapplies section 69. The claimants showed particular disadvantage and thereby satisfied section 69(2). Thereafter the burden was on Next to justify the factor under section 69(1)(b). And, as is clear from the case of McNeil v Revenue and Customs Commissioners [2018] ICR 1529 (“McNeil”), if a claimant shows that a factor puts persons of their sex at a particular disadvantage, it is not open to the employer to seek to show that the disadvantage was not caused by their sex.
As for ground 15, Mr Short submitted that the ET made a proper and sufficient factual comparison between the advantaged and disadvantaged groups, that the same proportionality test applies to an “equal value” case as applies to a “like work” case and that the ET at paragraph 258 dealt with the fact that there was no absolute barrier to any of the claimants moving to warehouse work.
Discussion
Ground 11 plainly succeeds in light of my ruling that the ET erred in finding that Next did not have a legitimate aim. That error unbalances the proportionality analysis. If that were the only error, the exercise would have to be re-done.
Turning to the other grounds, I make the general observation that the brevity of the ET’s analysis in paragraph 270 of the judgment makes the appeal against the proportionality ruling more difficult for the claimants to resist. All of the emphasis in the ET’s decision was on the finding as to legitimate aim and, as a result, there is only the briefest analysis of proportionality. That is all the more striking in light of the comments in Hardy to which I referred above. On one view that brevity could make it harder for this Tribunal to carry out the necessary careful scrutiny of the ET’s decision. On another, it could mean that that careful scrutiny may itself be briefer or more briefly expressed.
Grounds 12 and 13, in my judgment, are well founded.
As I have already said, Next paid a higher market rate for warehouse work because of recruitment and retention factors which did not apply to the retail workers. Therefore this was not a case of simply paying more for what was perceived by the market as typically men’s work.
As Mr Green said, it is entirely clear from Enderby that a pay differential arising from a need to attract candidates to a role can be justified. It is a question in each individual case whether it is justified.
In paragraph 270 the ET said that reliance on market forces as a trump card would allow lower pay in particular sectors due to indirect discrimination to be sustained in perpetuity and, therefore, “there must usually be a more compelling business reason for such arrangements to be justifiable”. In my judgment, that approach was not in line with the guidance in Enderby. The potential for reliance on market forces was unduly restricted by the imposition of a “more compelling business reason” test.
In addition, some of the specific errors to which I referred above in respect of legitimate aim were relevant again. The reference to “lower basic pay” was not a fair reflection of what happened, i.e. the payment of higher basic pay to one group for reasons which did not apply to the other group. The reference to “financial headroom” again suggested that the ET was considering the affordability of equalising the pay instead of assessing the reason for the difference in pay.
For those reasons it seems to me that “trump card” was not a fair characterisation of Next’s case. This was not a case where warehouse workers were paid more simply because warehouse workers tend to be paid more. That sort of application of market factors no doubt could cause discriminatory practices to be embedded. But paying more to warehouse workers for recruitment and retention reasons – as per the ET’s finding at paragraph 247 – was different. It might coincidentally help to preserve higher levels of pay in a sector which at one time had been male-dominated, but the point is that that was not all that it was doing. And the fact (if it was a fact) that Next could have afforded to equalise the pay of the retail workers did not, in my judgment, mean that the business need for the higher pay was not sufficiently great to outweigh its discriminatory effect.
Instead, I conclude that the ET’s findings of fact including those at paragraph 247 led to the conclusion that the pay differential was a proportionate means of achieving a legitimate aim. Next paid the rates to warehouse staff which it needed to pay for sound business reasons, and no more, and those business reasons did not apply to the retail staff.
In light of that ruling, I do not consider that anything is added by ground 14 and the alleged failure by the ET to assess any extent to which the difference in basic pay was caused by any discriminatory effect, if indeed that would be a legitimate area of inquiry following McNeil.
I am also not persuaded that there is merit in ground 15. Although I have disagreed with some of the ET’s conclusions of law, it does not seem to me that the ET failed to understand the essential facts of the case. It noted correctly that the effect of the statistics was not straightforward. There is no sign that it treated this case as if it were based on a PCP which created a barrier to entry to the advantaged group. And I am not convinced that cases based on “like work” and those, like this one, based on work of equal value, necessarily call for a different analysis.
The other contract terms and Ground 16
It is convenient to take these term by term, grouping the submissions and discussion under a single heading in each case, though some themes will become repetitive.
Those submissions and discussion cover issues which were raised about legitimate aim and proportionality. Mr Green further submitted that the errors which he identified in respect of the finding of Particular Disadvantage also infected the ET’s decisions on the other terms but, as I have already found against Next on that issue, I say no more about it here.
Unconsolidated Awards (term 2)
The ET found that at intervals during the relevant period, warehouse operatives were entitled to receive small payments ranging from £25 to £100. Sales consultants did not receive them. These one-off payments had been negotiated with the trade union to conclude deals. This enabled Next to avoid paying additional basic pay, providing a lower base for the next year’s negotiations.
The ET ruled:
“294. The character of the payment is so closely aligned to the underlying basic pay of warehouse workers that we are satisfied it falls on the wrong side of the costs only/costs plus demarcation line. The terminology of the aim as business performance and development and additional involvement of collective bargaining does not cloak the aim with legitimacy.
295. Had we found the aim to have been legitimate, we would have considered the factors to have been a proportionate means of achieving the aim. No obvious lesser measure was identified.”
Mr Green submitted that since the ET equated these payments so closely with basic pay, the errors identified above in relation to basic pay must also apply to this term.
In the alternative he submitted that on the ET’s own findings, the purpose of unconsolidated awards was to keep the basic pay of warehouse staff down while still achieving a deal with the trade union (a reason which did not apply to sales consultants) and that combined aim was plainly legitimate. The decision was also inconsistent with the ET’s decision on Long Service Awards (term 17), where they found that although the term was not proportionate, the aim of ensuring that a deal was reached with the union was legitimate.
In response Mr Short submitted, in addition to his submissions on basic pay which I have addressed above, that the ET was entitled to characterise Next’s aim for unconsolidated awards as it did.
In my judgment the lawfulness of term 2 stands or falls with that of basic pay. These small payments were simply part of the pay package of the warehouse staff, paid in one way so that they would not have to be paid in another way.
As with basic pay, what requires scrutiny is the difference between the treatment of the claimant and comparator groups. Whilst making these lump sum payments may have had the ultimate aim of reducing the wages bill for warehouse staff, that was not the reason why they were made to one group but not to the other. Next did what it did as a result of collective bargaining with the union which applied to warehouse pay but not to the pay of store consultants.
For the same reasons as apply to basic pay, with the additional element of collective bargaining, I find that the ET was wrong to characterise Next’s aim as “costs only” and it could not be so characterised.
Sunday Pay Premium (term 4)
The ET found that Sunday pay premium was paid at 25% to warehouse operatives who started before October 2006. For those starting between then and 2017 it was 15%. In 2017 it was removed for new starters but those already entitled continued to receive it.
For sales consultants starting prior to November 2001, Sunday pay premium was 50%. For those starting between November 2001 and June 2006, it was 25%. For those starting between June 2006 and 30 September 2008, it was 10%. For those starting on or after 1 October 2008, no Sunday pay premium was paid. In June 2015, Sunday pay premium was removed for all sales consultants previously receiving it at any rate. They received a payment calculated at one quarter of any Sunday pay premium received in the previous 12 months.
The evidence was that benchmarking of warehouse pay revealed that some employers paid extra for Sunday work but many did not. Meanwhile, in 2016 and 2017 many employers funded the increase from NMW to national living wage by reducing Sunday pay rates. The reduction in the rate and the removal for new starters in 2017 were agreed with USDAW. The ET said at paragraph 308:
“The second respondent was not in a position to remove the rates for Sunday pay for warehouse operatives recruited before this date, however reducing the rates for future employees represented a cost saving measure which would have increasing effect with the turnover of warehouse operatives each year.”
On the retail side, the ET summarised the evidence:
“Mr Mason said that the market drove the changes. He said no new starter could get a job in that market and receive a Sunday premium. By the time it was abolished in June 2015, only 1 out of 10 were still receiving it on a legacy basis and that seemed inequitable.”
Having found legitimate aims, the ET ruled at paragraph 316 that paying higher Sunday pay to warehouse staff who had a legacy entitlement to it, but not to retail staff, was not proportionate because there was no business need for the payments. That was on the basis that after the premium was stopped for new starters in 2017, there was no evidence of an effect on Sunday attendance thereafter. As it had said at paragraph 315:
“The respondents assert the proportionality arises from different occupational requirements for different labour markets without establishing on the evidence what they were: the reality is both markets require staff to work on Sundays.”
Mr Green submitted that the ET in making that finding made the errors identified in grounds 11-15 or similar errors.
Under ground 16, he further submitted that the ET irrationally disregarded its own specific findings that (a) there had been a change in the market and expectations for Sunday pay in the period to 2017 (307, 308, 313) and (b) Next “was not in a position to remove the rates for Sunday pay for warehouse operatives recruited before this date”, and (c) the fact that all of the comparators were recruited before 2017.
In response Mr Short noted the ET’s careful analysis of the facts and finding of a separate legitimate aim of encouraging work in unsocial hours, and submitted that the ET was entitled to make its factual finding of a lack of proportionality.
In my judgment it was not Next’s case that there was a continuing business reason for a Sunday pay premium. That is inherent in its decision to stop the premium for all new starters, in both sectors. Instead, the reason identified for continuing legacy payments to warehouse staff but not to retail staff was collective bargaining. At paragraph 315 the ET had said: “The effect of union representation may explain the better outcomes for warehouse workers in this area, but that is not really to the point.” But in my judgment it was to the point, the point being that Next was “not in a position” to remove the legacy payments.
In respect of this term I cannot reach a final conclusion as to what the right outcome on proportionality should have been, though it should be noted that reliance on collective bargaining outcomes for some other terms was judged to be proportionate. However, the ET’s explanation of its decision was not consistent with its findings of fact, and ground 16 succeeds in this respect.
Conversely, I am not persuaded that grounds 12 and 13 (which I have upheld in relation to basic pay) also apply to term 4.
Night Time Premium (term 5)
Different rates for night-time working were paid to warehouse staff and retail staff at different times and the differences were not necessarily less generous to the retail staff. However, the ET focused on a change which took place on the retail side in November 2012. Previously night-time premium was paid for hours worked between 9pm and 7am for those contracted to work such hours prior to April 2002 and, in all other cases, for hours worked between 10pm and 6am. But from November 2012 it was paid only for hours worked between midnight and 5am for all sales consultants.
Meanwhile, night-time premium was paid to warehouse operatives for hours worked between 10pm and 6am throughout the relevant period.
Night-time work was held to be critical to the warehouse operation. That was not the case for the retail operation, but during sales periods the stores had heavy trade. They opened from 5am. At paragraph 321 the ET found, in respect of the sales consultants:
“The change in the classification of night-time hours from up to 6am to 5am was designed to make savings because every employee would work two days a year during those sales period. The rationale was not that this was night-time work but starting earlier.”
The ET held that the change from 6am to 5am for retail staff was solely to save cost and this aim could not be legitimate.
Mr Green submitted that as with basic pay, the ET erred by looking solely at the reason for not paying the claimants more, rather than the reason for paying the night time hours for warehouse staff, having found that night-time work was critical to the warehouse operation.
He further submitted that the ET made the same error in its approach to characterising Next’s aims as was characterised in grounds 2 (fair characterisation) and 11 (outcome vitiated by earlier errors).
He further submitted that in deciding that term 5 was not proportionate, the ET again made the errors identified in grounds 11-15 or similar errors.
By ground 16, Mr Green further contended that the ET’s approach to proportionality was also irrational because it disregarded the fact that the need to recruit and retain sufficient warehouse operatives willing to work night shifts was a rationale for paying a night shift premium between 5 and 6am in the warehouses which did not apply to retail staff, and it was not contended that the hours could not otherwise be filled.
In response, Mr Short emphasised that the analysis of Next’s aim as costs saving was based on very different facts from the analysis in respect of basic pay, and it does not follow either that the same mistakes were made in both exercises or that the outcome should be the same.
I agree with Mr Short. Until November 2012, night-time work extended until 6am for both categories of employee (save those warehouse operatives with a legacy entitlement to night-time premium up to 7am). The change was to the disadvantage of the store consultants and the reason for the change was to save money. That finding of fact and the characterisation of the aim as “costs only” were open to the ET on the evidence. In my judgment, the differences between the need for night-time work in warehouses and stores respectively, though expressly recognised by the ET, were not found to be the reason for any difference in treatment.
I therefore reject grounds 2, 11 and 16 in respect of term 5, and the other grounds based on proportionality do not arise.
Overtime Premium (term 13A)
In the Grounds of Appeal and in counsel’s skeleton argument it is submitted that the ET’s findings on this term were subject to the errors of law identified in grounds 11 to 15. That contention has not otherwise been developed in submissions on either side. The question for me appears to be whether my findings on proportionality in respect of basic pay translate across to overtime premium.
The ET found that for additional hours above full-time equivalent, warehouse staff were paid either time and a half or double time depending on certain variables. Sales consultants, up to 12 October 2013, were paid a 50% premium for hours worked over 39 hours but after that date, no premium was payable.
Next’s evidence was that in fact, no store consultants were earning the premium which was payable up to 12 October 2013. But in the warehouses there were peaks in demand which were hard to predict, and overtime premium rates were offered to provide the necessary flexibility.
Having identified legitimate aims (aims 1 and 3), the ET held at paragraph 381:
“In the one instance there was a business need for overtime and in the other there was none. The discriminatory effect was notional given that sales staff were not required to work in excess of 39 hours. Nevertheless, to cover the eventuality that overtime might, exceptionally, be required in retail, there should be equivalence of terms. It was not reasonably necessary to meet the aim to maintain the differential rates. The defence under section 69(1)(b) is not established.”
I do not consider that ground 11 reads across to this issue. Nor does ground 12, which was concerned with the treatment of market forces. I have already rejected grounds 14 and 15.
That leaves the rationality ground 13, but that ground in respect of basic pay is strongly tethered to the recruitment and retention factors which led Next to pay higher rates to warehouse operatives. I am not persuaded that that ground can be read across to term 13A either.
The outcome on term 13A does leave a sense of unreality. Since there has for many years been no need for any overtime in the stores, it seems odd that it is unlawful not to have an overtime clause for retail staff. But I have not heard any technical argument which persuades me that section 66 of the 2010 Act – the section which reads a sex equality clause into a claimant’s contract – does not have the effect which the ET found it to have, even if that ruling has no practical consequence.
Paid Rest Breaks (term 16),
The ET found that during the relevant period, warehouse operatives were entitled to paid rest breaks based on the length of their shifts. Sales consultants were not paid for rest breaks. The evidence was that in the early 2000s, following the introduction of the NMW, paid rest breaks for retail staff were removed and working hours were modified as a trade-off. Next also adduced evidence that unpaid rest breaks were an industry standard in retail. On the warehouse side, the evidence was that breaks were negotiated with the trade union and reflected the nature of the work, though the ET observed that that would not explain why they were paid or unpaid. It accepted that payment for rest breaks to warehouse staff achieved the aim of viability, resilience and successful business performance by reflecting the market standard, but not that it met the aim of incentivising warehouse productivity. It found that the aim of removing payments to the retail staff was solely about cost, to meet the increase in the NMW, and was not legitimate. In any event the proportionality test was not satisfied because it was not reasonably necessary to restrict payment only to warehouse operatives to meet the aim.
Mr Green submitted that the ET erred by looking only at the desire to save cost on the retail side rather than the rationale for giving paid breaks to warehouse staff, namely the fact that they “were negotiated with USDAW and reflected the repetitive and monotonous nature of the tasks of warehouse operatives” (judgment paragraph 396). This repeated the errors in the treatment of basic pay, and it was also irrational to find reliance on ensuring a negotiated agreement with the trade union illegitimate for this term when it was held legitimate in relation to Long Service Awards (see term 17 below).
He further submitted that the ET made the same error in its approach to characterising Next’s aims as was characterised in grounds 2 and 11.
He further submitted that in deciding that term 16 was not proportionate, the ET again made the errors identified in grounds 11-15 or similar errors.
Under ground 16, Mr Green further contended that the approach to proportionality was irrational in light of facts established by unchallenged evidence i.e. agreement with the trade union, payment to reflect the nature of the warehouse work and the higher proportion of longer shifts in the warehouses, the trade-off between different terms for the retail staff and retail industry standards.
Mr Short responded that this is a very clear example of a “costs only” aim, where a benefit was removed from a group of employees in order to fund NMW. Here too the arguments are different from those relating to basic pay.
As in the case of Night Time Premium, I agree with Mr Short that the removal of the benefit from the retail staff overshadows the reason for continuing to provide it to warehouse staff. From the evidence the ET was entitled to conclude that its removal – and therefore the difference between the terms of the two groups of employees – was a costs saving measure. It was not bound to conclude from the evidence that the difference was because of the different business needs, though those differences existed. The appeal therefore fails in respect of this item.
Long Service Awards (term 17)
During the relevant period Next had systems of awards for long service for both warehouse and retail staff. The sums were not large, and the differences between awards for warehouse staff and retail staff were small and narrowed further after some changes in January 2020, but the warehouse scheme was slightly more generous. The ET accepted Next’s evidence that “the differences arose from negotiation with USDAW with respect to agreeing an overall package of remuneration” and that no such collective negotiations occurred with retail staff. It found that the payments were an appropriate means of meeting the business need of ensuring that a negotiated agreement with the union would be acceptable to its members, but that in the absence of a good reason for aligning the pay of the two groups earlier or completely, proportionality was not established.
Mr Green submitted that in deciding that term 17 was not proportionate, the ET made the errors identified in grounds 11-15 or similar errors.
By ground 16, he further submitted that the ET in its balancing exercise did not have regard to the very small size of the difference in pay, or to the more favourable terms for long service which retail staff had enjoyed up to 2014, or to the fact that the small payments to warehouse staff had been negotiated with the trade union as part of the overall package.
Mr Short submitted that collective bargaining is a process, not an aim, and that the ET reached the right decision because the differences between the pay of the two groups were unexplained. He also pointed out that the partial equalisation of the schemes in 2020 showed that there was no good reason for it not having happened earlier.
In my judgment this is another example of the unhelpful nature of the distinction between factors, aims and reasons for reliance. Whilst section 69 requires that analysis to be made, the key question was why the two groups received different awards. The ET’s answer was that Next needed to ensure a successful outcome to the negotiations with the trade union. That reason applied to the warehouse staff but not to the retail staff. Properly analysed, this was another instance of a decision to pay the warehouse staff more, rather than a decision to pay the retail staff less. It was therefore an error to require Next also to justify its omission to equalise the payments for retail staff (earlier or completely). Bearing in mind also the very small size of the differences (typically £5-10 per year in those cases where a difference occurred), I conclude that the ET’s ruling on this term cannot stand.
The cross-appeal: ground 1
The claimants’ submissions
Ground 1 of the cross-appeal challenges the ET’s rejection of the claimants’ case on direct discrimination under section 69(1)(a), i.e. the finding that differences in pay were because of a material factor reliance on which “does not involve treating A less favourably because of A's sex than the responsible person treats B”.
Mr Short does not contend that there was any error in the ET’s finding that the internal conscious or subconscious attitudes, intentions or mental processes of Next’s decision makers were free of any sex discrimination. Rather, he submits that the ET should have asked itself whether the market forces on which Next relied were themselves affected by stereotypes which were discriminatory on grounds of sex. This is relevant to the ET’s decision in Next’s favour in respect of basic pay and in respect of bonuses (terms 6, 7 and 8).
The issue is whether that question properly arises under section 69(1)(a) or under section 69(1)(b).
Mr Short’s starting point was the difference between section 13, the section which deals generally with direct discrimination on grounds of a protected characteristic, and the equal pay provision in section 69(1)(a) of the 2010 Act.
Section 13 outlaws direct discrimination where a person is treated less favourably “because of a protected characteristic”, but section 69(1)(a) requires a tribunal to ask whether reliance on the material factor “does not involve treating A less favourably because of A’s sex …”. Mr Short submitted that under section 69(1)(a), the focus is on the factor itself rather than the reason for the employer’s treatment of the employee. Although case law recognises a broad equivalence between the concepts in the two sections, they are not identical. The employer has the burden of proving that the material factor itself was not discriminatory, and in that respect, he submitted, the reach of section 69(1)(a) is wider than that of section 13.
Mr Short relied on the cases such as Smith, Ratcliffe, Armstrong and Surtees, quoted at paragraph 168 above, which predated the 2010 Act but, he submitted, remain good law. He submitted that the ET erred by treating section 69(1)(a) as if it mirrored section 13 and by ruling at paragraph 210 of the judgment that “judicial explanations” following Ratcliffe had been “swept away by the clarity of section 69”.
Mr Short submitted that to satisfy the burden of proof, an employer must not merely show that it was not consciously or unconsciously motivated by sex, but must also show that each material factor was not influenced by sex to a more than trivial degree. He accepted that that could be difficult for employers in a market forces case, but that difficulty would be no more than a consequence of their own choice to align their pay with the market, and the issue would only arise in those cases where different markets had different gender profiles. In this case, he submitted, Next relied on market forces but made no attempt to show that those market forces do not discriminate against women.
The problem extends to the ET’s decision in Next’s favour in relation to bonuses because market forces were found to be part of the reason for the differential treatment in those areas.
For those reasons Mr Short submitted that the ET was bound to find in the claimants’ favour on that issue. To fail to proceed in that way would be to risk equal pay legislation being made less effective.
Next’s submissions
Next’s oral submissions on the cr0ss-appeal were made by Kathleen Donnelly KC. She submitted that the ET correctly directed itself that section 69(1)(a) requires the employer to prove the material factor that was relied on “and also that it is not because of the sex of the claimant” (paragraph 170). It found expressly that there was “no conscious or subconscious influence of gender” (paragraph 208). That finding distanced this case from Ratcliffe, where decision makers were found to have been “willing to take advantage” of the market paying lower “women’s rates” (as interpreted in Armstrong no.2 per Underhill P at paragraph 38), the ET having referred to that case as one type of direct discrimination.
Ms Donnelly submitted that ground 1 misstates or ignores the boundary between direct and indirect discrimination, which is all the more important because indirect discrimination can be justified but direct discrimination cannot. Ground 1 suggests that there is a difference between section 13 and section 69(1)(a) despite this Tribunal’s ruling to the contrary in McNeil per Simler P:
“Section 69(1)(a) mirrors the definition of direct discrimination in section 13 of the Act and subsections (1)(b) and (2) together mirror the definition of indirect discrimination in section 19. It is clear that they must be construed consistently (as was well established in relation to the predecessor legislation, and as emphasised recently by the Supreme Court in Essop/Naeem [2017] ICR 640).”
Construing section 69 in accordance with ground 1 would, Ms Donnelly submitted, subvert the statutory scheme, and would also impose on employers the impossible burden of disproving any discriminatory motivation in the decisions of other employers in the market – and that notwithstanding the ET’s rejection, in almost all respects, of the claimants’ expert evidence by which they had sought to prove that retail work is perceived as being women’s work and warehouse work is perceived as being men’s work and that this impacts market rates of pay.
In oral submissions Ms Donnelly focused on the ET’s reasons for its decision on the bonuses. These emphasised the importance of performance and efficiency as reasons for the bonus schemes in the warehouse, making it harder for the claimants to show a causal link with market forces. The ET found that the overall package for warehouse staff matched the market but that Next’s bonus schemes were atypical. Ms Donnelly also pointed to the ET’s clear findings that equivalent bonus schemes could not have been implemented for retail staff. That being so, she asked, how could sex be the reason for the differential treatment? And if a sex equality clause were imported, how could it operate? She submitted that the cross-appeal in respect of bonuses is an impermissible collateral attack on those positive findings.
Meanwhile, she pointed out, there is no challenge to the ET’s finding that the differential treatment, viewed as indirect discrimination, was objectively justified. That, she submitted, underlines the unreality of this ground of the cross-appeal.
Overall, Ms Donnelly submitted that the construction of section 69(1)(a) proposed by ground 1 is incorrect and is not supported by any caselaw. Instead the cases show that a finding of direct discrimination requires a mental element on the part of the employer.
Discussion
I am not persuaded that there is merit in ground 1 of the cross-appeal.
Although the words used in section 13 and section 69(1)(a) are not identical, it is clear, and well established by cases such as McNeil, that paragraphs (a) and (b) of section 69(1) are concerned with direct discrimination and indirect discrimination as consistently defined across the 2010 Act’s various provisions. Section 69(1)(a) will not be engaged unless there is less favourable treatment “because of A’s sex”.
At paragraph 194 of its judgment the ET rightly noted that section 69 contrasts in that way with its predecessor, section 1(3) of the 1970 Act, which did not distinguish between direct and indirect discrimination.
The test, whether the unequal treatment was “because of A’s sex”, is one of fact. It could be satisfied in a case of the Ratcliffe kind where decision makers were found to be willing to take advantage of the market paying lower rates to female workers, as the ET recognised at paragraph 194.
Perhaps a borderline case might arise if, on the facts, the discriminatory effect of market forces was evident but the employer showed that it did not know or seek to take advantage of it. That, however, is not this case.
For these reasons I reject the proposition that direct discrimination must always be found where an employer relies on a material factor of market forces and does not adduce evidence to prove that those market forces do not disadvantage those of either sex.
Mr Short submits that this leaves a gap in the protection afforded by equal pay legislation. The answer to that, in my judgment, is the requirement for objective justification in all cases of particular disadvantage. As can be seen from Enderby, whilst an employer can rely on market forces, the ultimate question will always be whether that reliance is justified in the circumstances of the case.
Moreover, on the ET’s findings of fact the direct discrimination claim could not have succeeded. At paragraph 206 it recorded Mr Short’s submission that retail pay was “suppressed because it is historically discriminatory on grounds of gender” and his reasons for inviting an inference that such factors played a part in the setting of basic pay. At paragraph 208 it rejected those submissions, making the decisive findings of fact to which I have referred above.
It is true that in the same paragraph the ET said: “Historic reasons for imbalances in pay for work which is equally valued fall into indirect discrimination considerations”. This ground of cross-appeal challenges that proposition. But even if the ET’s proposition were too widely stated and “historic reasons” are capable of forming part of a direct discrimination analysis, it does not seem to me that a real issue would arise on the facts of this case. Although the ET went on to find at paragraph 239 that Next had benchmarked “in a warehouse market with a largely male workforce” (see the discussion of Next’s ground 9 above), it did not make a finding that retail pay was suppressed by reason of historic discrimination on grounds of sex, and it had already substantially rejected the expert evidence adduced on the claimants’ behalf.
Ground 1 of the cross-appeal therefore fails.
The cross-appeal: ground 2
The claimants’ submissions
Ground 2 of the cross-appeal is advanced in the alternative. The claimants had invited the ET to infer that decision makers knew that they were setting rates of pay which were historically discriminatory on grounds of gender. At paragraph 207 of its judgment the ET set out ten factual matters on which it was suggested that that inference could be based, of which the final two were:
“207.9. The respondents have failed to call the relevant decision makers,
specifically Lord Wolfson or other members of the Board to discount any
influence the gender of the sales consultants played in the setting of pay
and, the burden of proof lying on the respondents, direct discrimination has not been disproved.
207.10. A failure to disclose relevant documentation against a history of
nondisclosure which led to an application to strike out the response,
providing fertile ground for the drawing of adverse inferences.”
The ET rejected that invitation, finding the evidence of Next’s witnesses to be “compelling” and to prove that “it was all about cost” and “gender did not enter into the equation” (judgment paragraph 208). The drive to reduce cost “would have happened regardless of the gender split in either market”. At paragraph 209 the ET concluded:
“In response, the claimants would say it does not matter what the respondents might have done, hypothetically, if the gender dimensions of the workforce were different. The fact was that a group of workers who were predominantly women were paid less for work of equal value than a group of other workers who were, albeit marginally, men. If the decision can in any part be attributed to taking advantage of a market rate which has historical sex taint the respondents have not established their defence. The answer to that is that we do not find that any part of the thought processes of Mr Mason and his colleagues when fixing the basic rate, or any aspect of, pay was that this was a group of workers who were in receipt of lower rates of pay because they were women. The attention was on the national minimum wage and how to achieve the necessary number of staff to discharge the sales service by paying as little as they could.”
The ET said that it had given “careful consideration” to the absence of Lord Wolfson or a member of the Board, who was the “ultimate controlling force” (paragraph 214). It cited this Tribunal’s decision in Scottish Water v Edgar [2024] EAT 32 for the proposition that evidence to explain a difference in pay may not be direct but can be circumstantial or “taken at second hand from a person who was suitably knowledgeable” (paragraph 216). At paragraph 217 it explained why it considered Mr Mason to be “well positioned” to give the necessary evidence.
The ET reviewed the history of disclosure issues and explained why it did not draw an adverse inference from the absence of certain documents.
Mr Short submitted that the ET’s conclusion was perverse, in the absence of any evidence from the relevant decision-makers or disclosure of the relevant documents. The case of Edgar, he said, arose where it had not been possible to identify the decision maker, and also it concerned causation but not mental processes. Mr Mason’s evidence was not a sufficient basis for the ET’s conclusion because it dealt only with the point at which pay proposals went to the Board and he could not speak to what happened at Board meetings. Next bore the burden of proof and therefore could not succeed without evidence.
Next’s submissions
Ms Donnelly emphasised the ET’s multiple, detailed and unappealed findings about the role of Mr Mason and his ability to give evidence about Next’s decisions on retail pay. See in particular paragraph 217:
“Mr Mason was at the centre of the process for yearly setting of pay levels
during the relevant period and was involved in all stages save for it being approved and signed off by the Board and any contact the Board might have had with the Finance department. He was well positioned to give evidence about those factors which did and did not influence the process in the extensive discussion he had with others, including Lord Wolfson, over the years. His explanations aligned with the evidence of Mrs MacIntyre and Mr Kelly, insofar as there were commonalities across the Group to setting pay by way of the use of benchmarking by market rates.”
In addition, paragraph 198 of Next’s skeleton argument contended:
“Similarly the Tribunal made unappealed factual findings as to the limited role of the Board:
(a) the retail budget established by Mr Mason was included in the budgets sent by the Finance Department to the Board ‘for approval and sign off by the Board of Directors’ (judgment 86);
(b) pay levels were ‘approved and signed off by the Board’ at (judgment 217); and
(c) ‘The Board’s role did not involve revising the pay proposals when signing off the budgets’ (judgment 223).”
The ET noted the claimants’ contention that Mr Mason’s evidence was not sufficient, considered it carefully and decided that it could safely make findings on the evidence it had heard.
In those circumstances Ms Donnelly submitted that the claimants came nowhere near the high threshold for a perversity challenge.
Discussion
I am also not persuaded by ground 2 of the cross-appeal.
There is no rule of law which states that an employer defending a decision must call the individual(s) who made the decision to explain it, or adduce documentary evidence which states or demonstrates the reasons for the decision.
Instead, the ET must decide the facts by weighing the evidence which the parties adduce. If there is no evidence from which a significant issue of fact can be resolved, then the party having the burden of proof on that issue will fail.
A party who does not adduce direct evidence from a decision maker therefore runs the risk of a negative outcome. That risk logically applies to any company which relies on a Board decision and does not adduce evidence from its Board.
However, it is permissible for the process of finding facts to include the drawing of inferences. An inference is a conclusion of one fact which can logically or reasonably be based on the evidence of another fact.
In this case the ET felt able to draw inferences about the reasons for the Board’s decisions, based largely on the evidence of Mr Mason. Its judgment specifies numerous detailed reasons why it considered that Mr Mason was well placed to give evidence about the setting of Next’s pay rates, including his being “at the centre of the process” and his having had “extensive discussion … with others, including Lord Wolfson”.
That inferential evidence had to be weighed against any positive evidence of direct discrimination. In this case there was none. From the ET’s judgment it is clear that the balance was tipped by an abundance of evidence from Mr Mason and his colleagues which supported the conclusion that sex had nothing to do with Next’s decisions on pay rates.
Logically there remained a possibility that the Board, behind closed doors, had engaged in direct discrimination. But there was no legal reason why the ET was bound to reject Next’s case that that had probably not happened.
This Tribunal will interfere with findings of fact only where it is absolutely clear that no reasonable ET could have made those findings. In my judgment the present case does not approach that threshold. Next relied on a detailed inferential case which the ET was entitled to accept, and it gave a detailed and convincing explanation of why it accepted it.
Nor do I consider that a lack of disclosure should have led to any different conclusion. A respondent which fails to preserve or produce a relevant document risks the drawing of adverse inferences or a failure to prove its case. But in this case the ET considered the claimants’ disclosure objections in some detail at paragraphs 222-225 of its judgment. It decided that on the facts of this case adverse inferences should not follow from a lack of documentation, and it then set about the task of deciding the facts on the basis of the evidence before it. It made no error of law in that regard.
Conclusion
The appeal succeeds to the extent set out above.
The cross-appeal is dismissed.
Further submissions will be invited on disposal and consequential matters.

items.summary: Colin Williams died at the scene after being crushed under an All Terrian Vehicle (ATV) Neither of the men in the ATV were wearing seatbelts or had received adequate training to safely use the vehicle Following the death of a farm employee in Monmouthshire after an ATV he was a passenger in overturned, the owner […]
items.body:
- Colin Williams died at the scene after being crushed under an All Terrian Vehicle (ATV)
- Neither of the men in the ATV were wearing seatbelts or had received adequate training to safely use the vehicle
Following the death of a farm employee in Monmouthshire after an ATV he was a passenger in overturned, the owner of the farm, Allen Roberts, has been fined £5500.
The ATV was being driven down a hillside at Wyesham, Monmouthshire, when the incident occurred on 25 August 2022. The driver of the ATV lost control of the vehicle and Mr Williams, 58, was ejected from the vehicle which did not have any doors.
He suffered fatal crush injuries and died at the scene.
An investigation by the Health and Safety Executive (HSE) found that neither Colin Williams or the driver of the vehicle had been provided with adequate training and neither of the men were wearing seat belts. The investigation also found that no routine pre-use checks were made on any of the vehicles owned by Allen Roberts that were used on the farm to ensure they were safe to use.
The investigation identified that the tyres of the ATV were improperly inflated, with differing pressures in each tyre, which should have been rectified before the vehicle was used. The vehicle was being driven in a high gear and two-wheel drive when it should have been in a low gear and four-wheel drive. The keys to the ATV were not adequately controlled and were available to anyone who was on the farm, including those not adequately trained.
Colin Williams was the only employee of Hill Farm and he was being assisted by the driver of the ATV in the clearance of vegetation and trees from a farm access route.
HSE guidance states employers must provide employees who use All-Terrain vehicles (ATV’s) with adequate training and instruction on their safe use. Any operators using the ATV owned by Allen Roberts should have received training in the safe method of operating the type of terrain that was present on the farm and should have been instructed to wear seatbelts where there was a foreseeable risk of overturn. There should have been a system for pre-use inspections to be carried out to ensure defects were identified and remedial actions taken before the vehicle was used.
Allen Roberts, of Hill Farm, Monmouth, pleaded guilty to an offence under Section 2(1) of the Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974. He was fined £5500 and ordered to pay £5813 in costs at Merthyr Tydfil Magistrates’ Court on 2 September 2026.
HSE Principal Inspector Damian Corbett said the dangers associated with ATVs in agriculture and forestry were well known.
“Anyone operating these machines should have the right training and be wearing seat belts when travelling,” he said.
“This accident was a tragic consequence of a lack of training, and a lack of basic safety precautions which cost a family a husband and a father.
“Employers must ensure that those entrusted to operate vehicles are properly trained and instructed to wear seat belts or safety equipment where there is a risk.”
The prosecution was brought by HSE Enforcement Lawyer Julian White and Paralegal Officer Gabrielle O’Sullivan.
Further information

items.title: Baked goods company fined £333,333 after worker suffers broken arm
items.summary: Worker suffered multiple fractures after arm was caught in unguarded conveyor machinery. HSE investigation found the company failed to prevent access to dangerous parts of machinery. HSE guidance explains employers must take effective measures to prevent access to dangerous machinery. A baked goods manufacturer has been fined £333,333 after a worker suffered multiple fractures, including […]
items.body:
- Worker suffered multiple fractures after arm was caught in unguarded conveyor machinery.
- HSE investigation found the company failed to prevent access to dangerous parts of machinery.
- HSE guidance explains employers must take effective measures to prevent access to dangerous machinery.
A baked goods manufacturer has been fined £333,333 after a worker suffered multiple fractures, including a broken arm when it became entangled in a sausage roll conveyor line.
Ribeca Jesuthasan was working for David Wood Baking Limited at the company’s food manufacturing factory in Sheerness, Kent, on 1 December 2023.
Ms Jesuthasan was cleaning a sausage roll production line when she passed her hand through an unguarded conveyor roller. Although the conveyor line had initially been switched off, it began to operate while she was cleaning it.
Her arm was pulled into the rotating roller, causing multiple fractures.
An investigation by the Health and Safety Executive (HSE) found that David Wood Baking Limited had failed to prevent access to the rotating parts of the sausage roll conveyor line.
Employers have a legal duty to take effective measures to prevent access to dangerous parts of machinery. This will normally involve the use of fixed guarding. Where routine access is required, interlocked guards may be necessary to prevent dangerous parts moving before a person can reach the danger zone.
HSE guidance, A recipe for safety: Health and safety in food and drink manufacture (HSG252), covers the main health and safety hazards in the food and drink industries and provides practical advice on how to manage the associated risks.
David Wood Baking Limited of Calverley Road, Leeds, pleaded guilty to breaching Regulation 11(1) of the Provision and Use of Work Equipment Regulations 1998. The company was fined £333,333 and ordered to pay £7644 in costs at Medway Court on 1 September 2026.
HSE inspector Delcina Burden said:
“Too many workers are seriously injured every year as a result of contact with dangerous parts of machinery due to inadequate or absent guarding.
“If simple measures had been taken, this incident could have been avoided.
“The sentence handed down by the court in this case should demonstrate that the courts and HSE take breaches of health and safety law seriously. We will not hesitate to take action against companies that fail to do all they can to keep people safe.”
The HSE prosecution was brought by HSE enforcement lawyer Iain Jordan, paralegal officer Anushka Lulith, and prosecution advocate Ruksana Begum.
